# Abstract

The rapid expansion of computing infrastructure driven by large language models has raised questions regarding the local economic and environmental footprints of data centers. Empirical research remains hampered by expensive, proprietary data aggregators that obscure historical entry timing and facility locations. This paper addresses that bottleneck by introducing an open-source, reproducible time-series data pipeline that leverages federal statistics under the North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) 518 classification across all contiguous U.S. counties from 2007 to 2022. We evaluate local economic effects by pairing staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) specifications with machine learning methods used for structural feature engineering, spatial impact modeling, and counterfactual simulation via Conditional Variational Autoencoders (CVAEs). Our spatial approach estimates nearby data center exposure using overlap-weighted 50-mile county buffers, allowing the analysis to account for potential spillover effects across county boundaries. Unsupervised clustering shows that data centers are predominantly an urban phenomenon, challenging the common notion of remote rural placement. However, measurable economic impacts are largely concentrated within rural counties. In these rural communities, data center exposure is associated with mixed outcomes: lower local unemployment rates, increased single-family construction permits, and localized decreases in $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ fine particulate matter, while simultaneously correlating with declines in average personal income and contractions in traditional industrial employment. These results indicate that data center development brings local trade-offs rather than uniform economic gains, providing researchers and regional planners with an accessible framework to evaluate infrastructure growth.
